claims.claim: A written WotC house style guide does exist for the 5e era: 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing', Version 1.04a ©2013 Wizards of the Coast, distributed to freelancers/Adventurers League authors and later bundled on the DMs Guild; it governs mechanics of style, not prose voice.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing v1.04a (PDF, 9 pp.)
claims.quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

claims.claim: The house style rests on the Chicago Manual of Style 16th ed. and Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th ed., with the guide covering only D&D-specific departures.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: The Chicago Manual of Style, 16th edition

claims.claim: Rules text is written in the second person, which the guide presents as the standard way to achieve gender neutrality; singular 'they' is banned outside dialogue and 'he/she' alternation is forbidden.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person

claims.claim: 5e inline subheads (heading 4) end in a period rather than the colon used in earlier editions, e.g. 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency...'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.claim: Game quantities always take numerals ('3 hit points', '1 round', '30 feet') while narrative distances and durations follow Chicago and are spelled out ('fifty miles', 'six hours').
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: In rules writing, we use numerals more often.

claims.claim: The guide fixes a verb list for mechanics: you 'make' a saving throw that 'succeeds or fails', attacks 'hit or miss', you 'deal' and 'take' damage, 'regain' hit points, and 'must succeed on' (not 'must make') a check.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.

claims.claim: 5e abandoned the 3E/4E use of 'result' for the number rolled and 4E's 'save' for a successful saving throw; 'magic item' never 'magical item'; 'deals 10 fire damage' not 'points of damage'; 'hit point maximum' not 'maximum hit points'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: We have abandoned that practice.

claims.feature: capitalisation and italics of game terms
claims.claim: Ability scores, class features, skills, planes, feats and 'Dungeon Master' are capitalised; spells and magic items are italicised and treated as titles, distinct from the effects they create.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: The italicized terms are treated as titles

claims.claim: The only prose-tone guidance is a 'High Fantasy' paragraph: epic scope, teamwork over lone heroes, humour or tragedy permitted only if they would not seem out of place in Lord of the Rings or Game of Thrones.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

claims.claim: American spelling, serial comma required, possessive 's' after names ending in s ('Asmodeus's'), 'non-' hyphenated before fantasy races ('non-elf') but 'nonhuman', 'not' contractions encouraged, vertical lists introduced by a full sentence and colon.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: We require the serial comma.

claims.claim: Page references are avoided as error-prone; sections and sidebars are cited by quoted title and chapters by number.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Style Guide v1.04a
claims.quote: We avoid page references as much as possible.

claims.claim: Dungeon magazine (Paizo era) required read-aloud text to be a bare-bones area description that never references the viewer or presumes player action, banning phrases like 'you see' and 'as you enter the room'.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: it does not make any reference to the viewer

claims.feature: read-aloud text: no creatures, few sentences
claims.claim: Read-aloud text should exclude creatures (whose positions depend on circumstances) and only rarely run more than a few sentences; long descriptive passages belong in player handouts.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: should only rarely run more than a few sentences

claims.claim: The Dungeon house template keys each encounter as header/EL, mandatory Read-Aloud Text first, then General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Development and Treasure, with adventures of 5,000–15,000 words and about 10,000 preferred.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter

claims.claim: Dungeon guidelines tell writers an adventure is not a short story, to condense backstory in favour of PC involvement, and never to presume PC actions or railroad.
claims.source: Paizo/Dungeon staff, Dungeon Submission Guidelines (PDF)
claims.quote: an adventure is not a short story

claims.feature: boxed text length and person (official 5e guidance)
claims.claim: D&D Beyond's official column advises boxed text of roughly four sentences under 100 words, phrased as third-person scene statements rather than 'as you enter, you notice', limited to perceivable sensory detail and excluding PC feelings, villain monologues and non-mechanical game terms.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
claims.quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

claims.claim: Boxed text should describe only what characters perceive, treating everything sensed as 'appears to be' rather than asserting hidden facts.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond, 2019-11-06
claims.quote: Everything they sense 'appears to be' what it is

claims.claim: Chris Perkins says published adventure text should entertain the DM who reads it, seeding humour and Easter eggs so the DM is more inclined to run it, and hooks should appeal to 80–90% of players.
claims.source: Todd Kenreck, 'Chris Perkins on Writing Your Own Adventures', D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19
claims.quote: having had a few good laughs

claims.claim: The WotC House Style Guide bundle circulated to freelancers is summarised as: focus on the characters, include a credible threat, focus on the here and now and omit verbose backstories.
claims.source: Mike Shea, 'On Writing Adventures', Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17
claims.quote: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories.

claims.claim: Boxed text is descriptive text in the adventure book meant to be read aloud verbatim or paraphrased, interleaved with rules references, and the DM-facing text explicitly instructs when to read or skip it.
claims.source: Callison-Burch et al., 'Dungeons and Dragons as a Dialogue Challenge for AI', EMNLP 2022, Appendix B
claims.quote: Read the boxed text when you're ready to start.

claims.claim: McKenzie treats read-aloud text as the adventure's 'at rise' stage direction, typographically set apart and read verbatim, and dates its first appearance to The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, 'D&D Adventures as Tragedy', Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
claims.quote: hints of what may be done are given in this text

claims.feature: DM preference for boxed text (designer poll)
claims.claim: A Jeremy Crawford Twitter poll cited by McKenzie found 59.5% of DMs prefer occasional boxed text, 34.4% want lots, and about 6% want none.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 2023-12-18
claims.quote: occasional boxed text

claims.feature: read-aloud text function and NPC action
claims.claim: Grouling Cover describes module read-aloud text as passages the DM is instructed to read that usually describe location but sometimes narrate NPC action, and likens it to a videogame cut-scene.
claims.source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (McFarland 2010), pp. 64–66, 80
claims.quote: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read

claims.claim: Grouling Cover argues second-person address pulls players directly into the storyworld, situating and immersing them, drawing on Fludernik's narratology of second-person texts.
claims.source: Jennifer Grouling Cover, The Creation of Narrative in Tabletop Role-Playing Games (2010), pp. 21, 85
claims.quote: pulling them directly into the storyworld

claims.claim: Hines finds Tomb of Annihilation's text repeatedly uses 'tribal', 'exotic' and 'savage', and its Port Nyanzaru read-aloud leans on vague stereotypes (dinosaurs, bright clothing, click languages) rather than specific cultural detail.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
claims.quote: heavy, characteristic accent

claims.claim: Hines notes DM-facing text instructs voicing Chultans with a heavy accent and tongue clicks, and reads background wording like 'correctly ascertain its original purpose' as prose that frames ruins as needing outsider validation.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 2023-03-19
claims.quote: correctly ascertain its original purpose

claims.claim: Hewitt shows Curse of Strahd's Death House read-aloud builds gothic atmosphere through decay adjectives (moldy, rusty, gaunt, pale-faced, voluminous) in present-tense third-person description.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 2024-12-15
claims.quote: festooned with moldy skeletons

claims.claim: Jara analyses rulebooks as framing devices whose covers, prologues, epilogues and embedded fiction shape play; storytelling-game books open with atmospheric prologue fiction, whereas the 1974 D&D booklets used such framing far less.
claims.source: David Jara, 'A Closer Look at the (Rule-) Books', International Journal of Role-Playing 4 (2013)
claims.quote: notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs

claims.claim: Jara coins 'genesic framing' for rulebook text that discloses its own framing and incites players to produce further text, which he says accounts for the medium's persistence.
claims.source: David Jara, IJRP 4 (2013)
claims.quote: what I have called genesic framing

claims.claim: Macdonell argues the 1978 Tomb of Horrors' scripted descriptions and its illustration booklet are dissonant, producing interpretive ambiguity, and that later editions removed the visual assets (abstract only; full text paywalled).
claims.source: Cameron Macdonell, 'Tomes and Tombs', Games and Culture, 2025
claims.quote: visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity

claims.claim: Monte Cook characterises AD&D's house voice as heavy passive voice, stream-of-consciousness digressions, an advanced vocabulary and an authoritative, treatise-like tone that legitimised the hobby.
claims.source: Monte Cook, 'How you say it', Substack, 2021-07-27
claims.quote: the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions

claims.claim: The community term 'High Gygaxian' (coined by Maliszewski) names Gygax's archaic, thesaurus-driven diction ('perforce', 'antithesis of weal'), long multi-clause sentences and baroque tone, fullest in the 1979 DMG and Vault of the Drow.
claims.source: James Maliszewski, 'High Gygaxian', Grognardia, 2009-02-19
claims.quote: a platinum word when one worth a copper would do

claims.claim: Akrasia argues AD&D's Latinate vocabulary ('milieu', 'dweomer', 'phantasm', 'eldritch') made difficulty part of the appeal, and that later TSR simplification of the language reduced that cachet.
claims.source: Akrasia, Akratic Wizardry, 2013-03-18
claims.quote: you had to be smarter than average to understand it

claims.claim: A close reading of S1 Tomb of Horrors finds elevated verbs ('precipitated' for dropped), room text that mixes mechanics with narrative so it needs re-reading, yet short punchy details.
claims.source: Gus L, Dungeon of Signs, 2017-04-21
claims.quote: Gygax was good at short punchy bits of detail

claims.claim: Stu Horvath (MIT Press, 2023) calls the 1979 DMG strange and deeply idiosyncratic, a singular authorial vision; Wieck (1989) says the 2e DMG became as much advice as manual; Taylor notes the 5e DMG spends 127 pages teaching a novice DM.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Dungeon Master's Guide' (citing Horvath 2023, Wieck 1989, Taylor/Black Gate)
claims.quote: strange and deeply idiosyncratic

claims.claim: Wikipedia's PHB synthesis records Turnbull (1978) calling OD&D 'ambiguous and muddled' against the coherent AD&D PHB, Schick (1991) on 2e spell descriptions bloating past 100 pages, Kelly (2014) on more polished writing, and Abbott (2024) on the 2014 spell chapter as a wall of text.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Player's Handbook'
claims.quote: an unrelenting wall of text

claims.claim: Games scholar Jaroslav Švelch sees the Monster Manual as modelled on medieval bestiaries but with precise figures; Turnbull praised its explanatory text for amplifying the statistics.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Monster Manual' (citing Švelch, Turnbull)
claims.quote: medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures

claims.claim: The 1977 Monster Manual placed stat lines on the same page as descriptions, and Ed Greenwood criticised Fiend Folio entries for offering strange appearances with no depth to their listings.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Monsters in Dungeons & Dragons'
claims.quote: there is no depth to their listings

claims.claim: Wikipedia credits The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan as the first D&D adventure with boxed read-aloud text, but the citation is a 2017 blog post by Merric Blackman, not a scholarly source.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan'
claims.quote: the first D&D adventure to use boxed

claims.claim: Reviewers cited on Wikipedia find Xanathar's marginal quips too modern in register, sounding like a cranky Redditor rather than a fantasy crime lord.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Xanathar's Guide to Everything' (citing Charlie Hall, Polygon)
claims.quote: feels a bit too modern

claims.claim: Kunzelman (Paste) reads Volo's authorship as a deliberate device letting the sourcebook include rumor and error, and Furniss praises its marriage of narrative and mechanical information.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Volo's Guide to Monsters' (citing Kunzelman, Furniss)
claims.quote: having Volo write the guide means that he can be wrong

claims.claim: A GeekDad reviewer cited on Wikipedia says reading Curse of Strahd front to back is like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book, and Black Gate calls it a setting manual and adventure in one.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Curse of Strahd' (citing Bristol, Jones)
claims.quote: like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book front to back

claims.claim: Evan Torner, cited on Wikipedia, describes 3e's design intent as Eurogame-style elegance in which terminology and choices should be immediately intelligible.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editions of Dungeons & Dragons' (citing Torner)
claims.quote: immediately intelligible to all who might play it

claims.claim: Rhodes argues the 2014 PHB left DMs to guess whether words were ordinary or mechanical, and that the 2024 PHB fixes this by capitalising game mechanics and adding an A–Z Rules Glossary.
claims.source: Duncan Rhodes, Hipsters & Dragons, 2025-03-10
claims.quote: just being used in their normal sense

claims.claim: The official 2024 PHB update renames race to species, 'Cast a Spell action' to 'Magic action', Inspiration to 'Heroic Inspiration', 'Use an Object' to 'Utilize action', folds shoving into Unarmed Strike, and adds glossary entries such as Ally, Enemy, Bloodied and Passive Perception.
claims.source: D&D Beyond staff, 'Updates in the Player's Handbook (2024)', 2024-09-03
claims.quote: Magic action

claims.claim: Screen Rant notes the 2024 Rules Glossary de-emphasises art with monochrome scenes to prioritise text and lacks a dedicated Conditions section.
claims.source: Ben Brosofsky, Screen Rant, 2024-09-21
claims.quote: the lack of a dedicated section for Conditions

claims.claim: Arndt reports the 2025 Monster Manual cuts iconic monsters' multi-page lore to at most three paragraphs and a roll table, adds a subtitle epithet to every monster, renames phylactery to 'spirit jar', and reads as a utilitarian encyclopedia.
claims.source: Dan Arndt, The Fandomentals, 2025-01-28
claims.quote: three paragraphs and a table to roll on

claims.claim: Shank's MA thesis characterises campaign-setting handbooks as giving encyclopedic knowledge of D&D geography, history and politics alongside ancillary rules.
claims.source: Nathan Shank, 'The Narrative Structures of Dungeons and Dragons', MA thesis 2011 (academia.edu, abstract/intro only)
claims.quote: encyclopedic knowledge of D&D geography, history, and politics

claims.claim: No stylometric, corpus-linguistic or authorship-attribution study of official D&D prose was found; searches on those terms returned only NLP actual-play datasets and generic stylometry papers, and the term 'Gygaxian' does not surface in Analog Game Studies, Games and Culture or IJRP indexes.
claims.source: Negative result from this sweep (searches 3, 22, 25, 35; Semantic Scholar rate-limited)

claims.claim: A written WotC house style guide exists — 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing' v1.04a (©2013), built on Chicago 16 and Merriam-Webster 11 — and it governs typography, numerals, verb collocations, capitalization and tone, with no rule at all on boxed/read-aloud text.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

claims.claim: A later revision, v1.08a (©2018, circulated as 'updated January 2019'), keeps the same structure (Chicago 17 now) and adds headings hierarchy, sidebar, gender-suffix, 'fellowship vs party' and edition-naming rules; it still contains nothing on boxed text or read-aloud prose.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: Avoid overusing sidebars.

claims.claim: The style guide was released publicly on DMs Guild around October 2018 as one of four free PDFs (IP guide, adventure guide, style guide, Forgotten Realms guide) that had previously gone only to official-play writers.
claims.source: EN World — DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game (thread, 2018-11-25)

claims.claim: On 2019-02-22 the DMs Guild account announced an updated House Style Guide listing for creators, noting it adds tips on gender-neutral language.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'Creators: Style Guide is now on DMsGuild!' (@dms_guild, 2019-02-22)
claims.quote: An updated #DnD House Style Guide is now on #DMsGuild

claims.claim: The Kind GM's post on the creator resource carries a May 2020 commenter report that the material was no longer available, which the author acknowledged — so the public window was roughly 2018–2020.
claims.source: The Kind GM — DMs Guild Style Guide Resources (2018-10-24)

claims.feature: house style guide (community says none published)
claims.claim: Community writers on either side of that window report no official guide: Half-Cover (2017) says WotC 'has not yet published the official style guide', Old Dungeon Master (2015) compiled one from 3.5/4e guides ('Perhaps they have one and I just couldn't find it'), and Blog of Holding (2025) says of the 2024 rules 'it annoys me not to have an official style guide'.
claims.source: Half-Cover — How to Follow the Writing Style of D&D (Michael, 2017-09-02)
claims.quote: has not yet published the official style guide

claims.feature: house style guide (community says none published, 2024 rules)
claims.claim: Paul Hughes built an unofficial 2024 style guide because no official one for the 2024 rules is available to the public.
claims.source: Blog of Holding — Unofficial D&D 2024 Style Guide (Paul Hughes, 2025-01-07)
claims.quote: it annoys me not to have an official style guide

claims.claim: Work-for-hire WotC freelancers receive the D&D House Style Guide, the 5e Word template, pitch examples and lore documents at contract start, and drafts are formatted with them.
claims.source: POCGamer — What happened? Writing for Wizards, Part 1 (Graeme Barber, 2021-03-23)

claims.claim: The official Adventurers League Dungeoncraft guide tells authors they must use the provided template and 'formatting standards as presented in the template' and be familiar with the D&D Style Guide, which it says is also provided.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide: The Wild Beyond the Witchlight, v1.2 (media.wizards.com)
claims.quote: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide

claims.claim: The 2023 Dungeoncraft Design Guide (effective 2023-11-09) again requires a specific template and familiarity with the D&D Style Guide; a poster frames this as organized play needing 'more guiderails than your usual table does'.
claims.source: EN World — D&D Adventurers League Unveils New DungeonCraft Document with Planescape In Focus (Raddu, 2023-11)
claims.quote: more guiderails than your usual table does

claims.claim: Kobold Press ran a 'Designing with Style' series that explicitly 'breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide', quoting its Common Pitfalls section verbatim — evidence the guide was public and treated as canonical by third-party 5e designers.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Designing with Style: Ability Checks and Saving Throws (Hannah Rose, 2019-05-31)
claims.quote: breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide

claims.claim: The guide's stated reason for second person in rules text is gender neutrality: 'In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: writing in the second person

claims.claim: v1.04a forbids 'they'/'their' as singular pronouns except in dialogue; v1.08a reverses this 'in a departure from our past usage' but tells writers to rely on it only when no pleasing alternative exists.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: but don't abuse this liberty

claims.claim: The guide fixes the game's verb idiom in a list: you cast a spell, deal damage, make a saving throw that succeeds or fails, make an attack that hits or misses, take damage, regain hit points, score a critical hit, use a feature.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails

claims.claim: Common Pitfalls: never write 'must make a DC 15 Strength check' unless success and failure are described next; the canonical form is 'must succeed on'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check

claims.claim: Third-party style guidance derived from the WotC guide: skill checks are always written as '[Ability Score] ([Skill])', outcomes are stated for success and failure, and multi-skill checks name at most two skills for brevity.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Designing with Style: Ability Checks and Saving Throws (Hannah Rose, 2019-05-31)
claims.quote: always written as [Ability Score] ([Skill])

claims.feature: numerals in rules vs words in narrative
claims.claim: Rules text uses numerals for any game quantity ('regains 3 hit points', 'lasts for 1 round', 'The room is 20 feet square') while narrative time and distance are spelled out ('slept for six hours', 'fifty miles apart').
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: the characters slept for six hours
claims.page: v1.04a pp.5-6, Numerals in Rules Text

claims.claim: The guide explicitly retires 4e usages: 'save' as 'successful saving throw' and 'result' as 'the number rolled on a die' — 'We have abandoned that practice.'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: We have abandoned that practice

claims.claim: Write 'deals 10 fire damage', not '10 points of fire damage'; write 'hit point maximum', not 'maximum hit points'; 'magic item' is never 'magical item'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: Avoid referring to points of damage

claims.claim: Capitalize ability scores, Armor Class, class features, Difficulty Class, feats, languages, planes, skills, racial/monster traits; italicize spell and magic-item names as titles (the spell wall of fire produces a wall of fire).
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)

claims.claim: Inline subheads (heading 4) end with terminal punctuation, not a colon — 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency…' — and are set in bold italics; bolded stat-block fields are a different thing.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.feature: no weeks or months in rules
claims.claim: Because a Realms week is a tenday, rules durations are given in days, never weeks or months (years are allowed).
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: say a game effect lasts for 7 days

claims.claim: The guide encourages contractions formed with 'not' (don't, can't, wasn't) and warns against ambiguous ones like 'who's' — a deliberately conversational register for rules.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)

claims.claim: The only tone guidance in the guide: D&D is high fantasy about small teams; humor or tragedy is fine if it doesn't overtake the tone, tested against Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones — 'ring wraiths aren't used for gags'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

claims.claim: v1.08a adds a diction rule: avoid 'fellowship' for adventuring groups because D&D companies are 'often fractious or more mercenary'; use group, band, company or especially 'party'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: often fractious or more mercenary

claims.claim: v1.08a switches from '5th Edition' to lowercase 'fifth edition', preferably as a modifier ('the fifth edition Dungeon Master's Guide').
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)

claims.claim: v1.08a: write 'priest', 'actor', 'god' regardless of gender; '-ess' forms only in in-world titles.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible

claims.claim: v1.08a requires descending the heading hierarchy without skipping levels, forbids inline subheads used merely for emphasis, and says the best sidebars 'can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)

claims.feature: in-world tenday rule vs WotC practice
claims.claim: A poster notes the style guide bans 'week' in favor of 'tenday' while WotC's own hardcovers violate the rule — house style is aspirational, not uniformly applied.
claims.source: EN World — DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game (thread, 2018-11-25)

claims.claim: Half-Cover infers from the books that spells and saving throws use 'very specific wording' and that features always spell out interactions (e.g., already having a cantrip), with fixed section order (starting equipment before class features).
claims.source: Half-Cover — How to Follow the Writing Style of D&D (Michael, 2017-09-02)
claims.quote: a strict style guide that all D&D sections adhere to

claims.claim: A community-compiled 5e writer's guide: 'Write in the present tense', avoiding 'will' for NPC/monster actions ('the golem attacks').
claims.source: Dungeon Master Assistance — D&D 5E Writer's Guide (Ronny, 2015-08-03)
claims.quote: Wherever possible, avoid using the future tense

claims.claim: In 2024 text, Bonus Action, Advantage/Disadvantage, Hit Points, Armor Class, Death Saving Throw, Proficiency Bonus, Challenge Rating and D20 Test are capitalized while ability, action, saving throw, skill, spell and feat stay lowercase; monster-name capitalization is inconsistent.
claims.source: Blog of Holding — Unofficial D&D 2024 Style Guide (Paul Hughes, 2025-01-07)

claims.claim: Justin Alexander: 2024 capitalizes defined terms (Cone, Target) to flag Rules Glossary entries, but definitions then live only in the glossary, scattering the targeting rules across pp. 236–238, 361, 364 and 376.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — D&D 5E 2024: Why Rules Glossaries Kinda Suck (2024-08-28)

claims.claim: 2024 condition text is standardized to mechanical statements — 'Your Speed is 0 and can't increase' replaces 2014's 'can't move' — and 'Utilize', 'Study', 'Influence' and 'D20 Test' become defined capitalized terms.
claims.source: Dungeon Master Assistance — D&D 5.5 PHB Review: Playing the Game and the Rules Glossary (Ronny, 2024-10-01)
claims.quote: Your Speed is 0 and can't increase

claims.feature: teach-first structure and annotated play example (2024)
claims.claim: The 2024 PHB opens with a How to Play chapter and a two-column example of play annotated with the applicable rules; Crawford frames the rewrite as 'teaching you how to play', contrasting 2014 which 'jumps right into character creation'.
claims.source: Wargamer — New DnD Player's Handbook aims to actually teach you the game (2024-06-18)
claims.quote: teaching you how to play

claims.claim: Idle Cartulary judges the 48-page rules section plus 18-page glossary 'absolutely stellar information design' and 'an incredibly confident book', though terms like Influence action lack definition where used.
claims.source: Idle Cartulary (Playful Void) — I Read The Player's Handbook (2024) (2024-08-31)
claims.quote: absolutely stellar information design

claims.claim: Mearls' 2013 Legends & Lore argument, as quoted: feat names like 'Rapid Shot and Precise Shot are abstract things that aren't really clear', whereas describing a fighter as an archer 'makes sense to anyone'; rules are 'a shared language'.
claims.source: Tenkar's Tavern — Mike Mearls' Latest Legends & Lore Column: Where Less is More (2013-03-03)
claims.quote: a shared language

claims.claim: A 2014 EN World thread infers that 5e designers chose rulings over exact language, which lets them 'use more natural language' — community inference from Mearls' videos, not a designer statement about prose.
claims.source: EN World — Design Philosophy of 5e (thread, 2014-06-25)
claims.quote: use more natural language

claims.claim: 5e core-book editor Scott Fitzgerald Gray: mechanics editing needs precision in how a book 'fits in with the game as a whole', narrative editing needs flow and pacing, and prose editing serves 'the emotional language of the game' so readers feel like a character in the world.
claims.source: Shadomain — Tales From the Tavern: Interview with Scott Fitzgerald Gray (2024-03-20)
claims.quote: the emotional language of the game

claims.claim: Perkins says every adventure for a decade had to re-explain doors, so the 2024 DMG codifies them; Wyatt calls re-explaining boxed text in every adventure a 'stupid little thing' the DMG (p. 9) now covers, pending the editing team.
claims.source: Screen Rant — After DM's Guide Preview, I'm Convinced Future D&D Adventures Will Drop These Two Repetitive Features (Ben Brosofsky, 2024-10-29)
claims.quote: stupid little thing

claims.claim: Perkins on the 2024 DMG: 'everything in there better be cracking on topic'; the sample adventures use 'tight and short' read-aloud scripts to jog the DM's memory, avoiding his earlier 32-page adventures.
claims.source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: tight and short

claims.feature: Curse of Strahd vs Storm King's Thunder boxed text
claims.claim: DMDavid observes Perkins boxed every location in Curse of Strahd, even empty rooms, and that his next adventure, Storm King's Thunder, 'omits almost all read-aloud text' — the two extremes of WotC 5e practice.
claims.source: DMDavid — How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, 2016-11-21)
claims.quote: omits almost all read-aloud text

claims.claim: Every 2025 MM entry opens with a single characterizing phrase ('tentacled subterranean trapper', 'guardian manifestation of the divine'); lore is 'compact but effective' though 'a little too compact for my taste'; quote boxes appear on some entries.
claims.source: EN World — Monsters & More: An In-Depth Review of the 2025 D&D Monster Manual (Beth Rimmels, 2025-01-28)
claims.quote: tentacled subterranean trapper

claims.claim: TheGamer: 'The flavor has amped up narratively, and the mechanics have followed' (angels wield light, kenku use shadow-magic daggers); there is no lore glossary.
claims.source: TheGamer — 2025 Monster Manual Review (Jerel Levy, 2025-01-28)

claims.claim: Xanathar's Guide carries 'little notes that run as commentary throughout the book, usually a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter', continuing the Volo's device but less relevant on a mechanics-heavy book.
claims.source: Skyland Games — Review: Xanathar's Guide to Everything (Scott D, 2017-11-13)
claims.quote: a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter

claims.claim: Dyson Logos, citing Decker and Noonan's 2005 GenCon table observations, holds that a DM gets two sentences before players stack dice; players missed dimensions, exits and monster counts in longer boxed text.
claims.source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)
claims.quote: you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: A 2025 EN World poster re-cites the 2005 Noonan/Decker WotC article: two sentences, 'DMs who didn't used boxed text had more engagement', cold reading is worse than personal phrasing, 'Ditch the boxed text and use your own words' — upstream article not fetched, single-lineage claim.
claims.source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
claims.quote: Ditch the boxed text and use your own words

claims.claim: Thread posters set ceilings of 'no more than two sentences' (GM Lent) or '3 to 5 sentences at most' with listed details for closer investigation (el-remmen).
claims.source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
claims.quote: 3 to 5 sentences at most

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin's D&D Beyond craft column: an opening should be 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words'; avoid 'paragraph after paragraph of boxed text'.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
claims.quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words

claims.claim: A 5e designer describes evolving from verbose 5e style to bullets to boxed text that is 'typically three lines, and never longer than five' because it sped play and set a base tone per room.
claims.source: Revivify Games — What I Value In Adventure Design (2025-03-04)
claims.quote: typically three lines, and never longer than five

claims.claim: Sly Flourish: a read-aloud is a tiny story told in 'less than 250 words'; if editing didn't remove 25% you didn't try; 'Keep it short and keep it powerful.'
claims.source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
claims.quote: less than 250 words to tell it

claims.claim: Outside introductions, a boxed text with a paragraph break 'isn't already too long by half' is rare; villain dialogue should be broken into ~six-second (one-round) statements.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
claims.quote: isn't already too long by half

claims.claim: Justin Alexander: 'boxed text is often too long'; break 'freeze-frame' text into actionable chunks and stop at the reaction point so players respond before the world moves on.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
claims.quote: boxed text is often too long

claims.claim: Gus L.: a basic room key is five sentences maximum; longer only for puzzles and NPCs — 'no one wants to read a three page key'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: no one wants to read a three page key

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch: long read-aloud at each location means 'the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones', even when, rarely, the prose is good.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)

claims.feature: third person over second person in boxed text
claims.claim: Merwin's core fix: 'Move from the second-person point of view to the third person' — 'The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing' instead of 'As you enter the clearing, you notice…' — so text cannot dictate PC actions or feelings.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Move from the second-person point of view to the third person

claims.feature: no dictated PC actions or emotions
claims.claim: Merwin's D&D Beyond rules: never 'as you approach' or 'you enter'; never 'stunned', 'terrified', 'heart pounds'; no game-mechanics terms used non-mechanically in boxed text.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)

claims.claim: Alexander names the pitfall 'remote-control text': 'You step forward', 'You smile', or declaring 'the thoughts or feelings' of PCs; show the scene, 'don't tell them how they're reacting to it'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
claims.quote: the thoughts or feelings

claims.claim: Dyson: bad boxed text 'predicts the future for the party (upon approaching…)' or commands behavior ('you stand in shock'); cure is one or two simple sentences or a point-form list.
claims.source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)
claims.quote: predicts the future for the party

claims.claim: DM's Workshop argues the opposite of Merwin: shift from third-person objective ('A 200-foot waterfall cascades') to second-person subjective ('You see a majestic waterfall') so the DM addresses the players rather than 'the empty air'.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
claims.quote: the empty air

claims.claim: Key-writing rule: 'Write without assumption of perspective' about entry point; use compass directions ('east wall'), never relative ones ('far side').
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)
claims.quote: Write without assumption of perspective

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons: keep descriptions 'short and punchy', don't tell players what to feel, use east/west not left/right, and let the map carry redundant door descriptions.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)
claims.quote: short and punchy

claims.claim: Readers summarizing Lynch's standards: don't provide conclusions, avoid 'if/then' constructs as padding, and don't address the party directly in read-aloud.
claims.source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)

claims.claim: Robin D. Laws: in hypothetical RPG text drop 'will' — 'If the agents reach the safe house, Keletny burns the car'; also avoid passive voice and 'to be' + verb pairs.
claims.source: Pelgrane Press — Five Keys to Punchier Prose (Robin D. Laws, 2012-02-01)
claims.quote: Keletny burns the car

claims.claim: Ray Vallese's editor's guide devotes a section to 'using present tense instead of future tense' and to 'avoiding rampant capitalization' — two habits of RPG manuscripts an editor corrects.
claims.source: Ray Vallese — Writing With Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers (book page)
claims.quote: using present tense instead of future tense

claims.feature: describe what can be sensed, not what can't
claims.claim: Merwin's epistemic rule: 'Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot' — no crate contents, but never omit the 50-foot chasm.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot

claims.claim: Words like 'seems' and 'appears' telegraph tricks: 'If something "appears to be" to the characters, it "is"' — let Perception checks, not hedges, create the distinction.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: If something 'appears to be' to the characters, it 'is'

claims.claim: Include only environmental details PCs will interact with; the smell of flowers can go 'unless you happen to be DMing for a party comprised solely of elves or florists'.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: a party comprised solely of elves or florists

claims.claim: 'Avoid the novelist/dramatist urge': no evil soliloquies, no coronation cutscenes; keep passages short and let PCs act.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Avoid the novelist/dramatist urge

claims.claim: 'Read your boxed text aloud to check readability' — tongue-twisters, unintended alliteration and odd phrasing are invisible on the page.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
claims.quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

claims.claim: Lynch's most-cited rule as summarized: replace the abstract judgment ('a cruel bully') with the concrete action ('Manfred takes a leak on Tobias's bedroll'); aim for 'the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait'; specificity, not mere detail.
claims.source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)
claims.quote: the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait

claims.claim: tenfootpole grades language on a four-point scale topped by 'Succinct and evocative', lists 'Terse writing style' and 'Evocative atmosphere' as requirements, and states 'Boxed text is usually not a good thing'.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Review Standards (Bryce Lynch)
claims.quote: Succinct and evocative

claims.claim: Lynch praises one 5e read-aloud for avoiding 'the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud' and for capturing a social scene in progress.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)
claims.quote: the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud

claims.claim: Skerples: use find-and-replace to hunt filler words ('little, big, grand, tall, dark') and swap in evocative choices; 'Every sentence needs to fight for its life in a dungeon key.'
claims.source: Coins and Scrolls — OSR: Sharpening the Axe: How I Plan and Write RPG Books (Skerples, 2019-09-05)
claims.quote: Every sentence needs to fight for its life

claims.claim: Gus L.: not 'evil idol' but 'toothy glare' or 'sharp edged obsidian'; include non-visual senses but never room history, future or emotions.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: sharp edged obsidian

claims.claim: Celeste Conowitch: 'keep it simple with a few powerful details' — the facts plus one detail ('reeks of garlic') that gives the room a story; never name the monster in narration.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Run your best actual play: Paint Me a Picture (Celeste Conowitch, 2026-07-20)
claims.quote: keep it simple with a few powerful details

claims.claim: Alexander's room formula: list notable things with positions, tag them with three of the five senses ('Try to include three of them'), then add a verb; NPCs get an action, clothing and one trait — 'you're not describing their headshot'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — Random GM Tip: Description Formulas (2022-02-08)
claims.quote: Try to include three of them

claims.claim: Anne K. Brown's essay (as reported): use all five senses and show rather than tell ('you detect orcs' is the failure), but don't over-invest in sensory prose players can't use.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.page: report on Brown, 'Listen! Do You Smell Something?'

claims.claim: Chris Doyle's essay (as reported): write read-aloud like a newspaper lead — immediate threat first ('GIANT SLAVERING OGRE'), secondary details after, lower-level details left for searching.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.quote: GIANT SLAVERING OGRE
claims.page: report on Doyle, 'How to Write Encounters that Don't Suck'

claims.claim: Sly Flourish: use fantastical language — 'quit writing read-aloud text that sounds like it came from Ikea instructions' — and make sure 'every word has a place in it'.
claims.source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
claims.quote: sounds like it came from Ikea instructions

claims.feature: punchy, emotionally slanted commercial boxed text
claims.claim: A review of dScryb's commercial boxed text finds it 'very punchy and to the point', carrying 'emotional information, motivations, or default assumptions' and sometimes 'selling' the creature or place.
claims.source: Gnome Stew — dScryb First Impressions (Rascher, 2021-07)
claims.quote: very punchy and to the point

claims.feature: active voice and expletive cuts (editor via critic)
claims.claim: Vallese's book, per Lynch: cut 'there is/are' openings ('An old wise man watches over the children'), prefer active constructions, and reorder stacked modifiers ('Its wormlike body is thin and scaly').
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: Its wormlike body is thin and scaly

claims.claim: Vallese: 'Do you have to follow all of these tips all the time? Nope… Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them' — vary to keep flavor and voice.
claims.source: Gnome Stew — Review: Writing with Style (J.T. Evans, 2017-10-23)
claims.quote: Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them

claims.claim: Laws' fifth key: use plurals to dodge gendered pronouns — 'Characters can leave their pistols at the door.'
claims.source: Pelgrane Press — Five Keys to Punchier Prose (Robin D. Laws, 2012-02-01)
claims.quote: Characters can leave their pistols at the door

claims.claim: BAATAG rule 7: replace 'to be' verbs with active ones and show rather than tell — describe details that reveal information through play.
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)

claims.claim: Merwin prefers the term 'narrative text': 'a series of prompts that can help your game flow more smoothly'; 'Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting' for atmosphere.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'This is exactly why boxed text is important' (Shawn Merwin, 2021-11)
claims.quote: Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting

claims.claim: Merwin (2019): 'A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text (well-written hopefully)' — omitting it is 'a risk', even though streamers rarely read it.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'What are your thoughts on boxed text?' (Shawn Merwin tweet, 2019-04-14)
claims.quote: A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text

claims.claim: Alexander rejects 3e's Traps/Creatures/Tactics/Development/Treasure key format because writers 'fill the format' and information lands out of play sequence: the ogre in the middle comes first, the goblin behind the tapestry does not.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — The Art of the Key (2014)
claims.quote: fill the format

claims.claim: The essential key: room title, boxed text ('seen in a glance'), reactive checks front-loaded, bold-titled significant elements, developing details from general to specific, a GM-background tag — and 'Complete sentences are overrated'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — The Art of the Key, Part 2: The Essential Key (2014-05-21)
claims.quote: Complete sentences are overrated

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons: first paragraph describes 'everything immediately observable' with interactables in bold; list contents in the order described; monsters go last in the first description but first in later keying.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)
claims.quote: Write a paragraph that describes everything immediately observable

claims.claim: Gus L.: '3 or 4 bolded words maximum' per complex room, each keyed to a follow-up paragraph; start with the room's inhabitants, then dangers, valuables, then hidden items tagged '(trap)' or '(hidden)'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: 3 or 4 bolded words maximum

claims.claim: BAATAG rule 2: no bullets or bolding by default — 'Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents'; later paragraphs are one topic each, recognizable from the first few words.
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)
claims.quote: Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents

claims.claim: Cygnus's rewrite format: name, a 1–2 sentence description touching several senses ('what the characters can immediately perceive'), listed interactables, nested details, stat lines last — explicitly to avoid long boxed text.
claims.source: The Lady and Tiger — Rewriting Dungeon Keys (Cygnus, 2023-11-30)
claims.quote: what the characters can immediately perceive

claims.claim: Tad Davis describes Campbell's economy method: bold for immediately visible items, arrows to hidden ones, indentation for stacking, omitting non-essential words, with sound/smell/breeze cues.
claims.source: ars phantasia — On Useful Dungeon Key Entries (Tad Davis, 2013-12-05)

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons cites Courtney Campbell's target of encoding 'everything you need to run successfully in seven words'.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)

claims.claim: Skerples: 'Cut mercilessly. Turn pages to paragraphs, paragraphs sentences, sentences to tables'; 'Sprawl is the enemy of utility'; begin with what is seen at a glance, then motion, smells, details, hidden information — never 'This room is…'.
claims.source: Coins and Scrolls — OSR: Sharpening the Axe: How I Plan and Write RPG Books (Skerples, 2019-09-05)
claims.quote: Sprawl is the enemy of utility

claims.claim: Gus L.: 'Maps! Use them.' — never spend key lines on dimensions and exits.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: Maps! Use them.

claims.claim: Gus L. rejects player-facing boxed text because it discourages referees from reading keys and is 'depreciating one big advantage RPGs have'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: depreciating one big advantage RPGs have

claims.feature: one-line keys vs the G1 pattern
claims.claim: DMDavid: Gygax 'usually wrote a 1-line note for each room' for Castle Greyhawk, but G1 (1978) gave 'generous descriptions for every location' and 'set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow'; length should match a location's purpose.
claims.source: DMDavid — How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, 2016-11-21)
claims.quote: usually wrote a 1-line note for each room

claims.claim: Jobe Bittman (as reported): give 'that which is necessary for the GM to run the scenario and have it make sense, and no more'.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.quote: and no more

claims.feature: subtext in adventure vs rules text
claims.claim: Monte Cook: adventure text states facts plainly and leaves the solution as subtext ('It's better unsaid'); setting text 'Don't be coy about the important stuff'; rules text never uses subtext.
claims.source: Monte Cook — Subtext in Game Writing (RPG Design Theories, 2022-12-22)
claims.quote: It's better unsaid.

claims.claim: Arnold K.: write snippets, run the dungeon to expose weaknesses, then cut — 'It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon'.
claims.source: Goblin Punch — How I Write An Adventure (Arnold K., 2017-01-27)
claims.quote: It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon

claims.claim: Lynch faults Vallese's guide for saying nothing about white space, bullets or evocative writing — the DM must 'glance at the page and immediately find' what is needed.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: glance at the page and immediately find

claims.claim: Perkins describes the 2024 DMG sample adventures' read-aloud as 'tight and short' scripts whose job is to jog the DM's memory, not to be recited.
claims.source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: tight and short

claims.claim: DMDavid: boxed text entered D&D with Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan, written for the Origins '79 AD&D tournament to give 'a consistent play experience in a competitive environment'.
claims.source: DMDavid — Picturing the dungeon: boxed text (David Hartlage, 2012-11-15)

claims.claim: 'When most speakers read something aloud, their voice takes a different tone and cadence than when they speak extemporaneously', so attention wanders; boxed text also dwells on 'the color of the sunset'.
claims.source: DMDavid — Picturing the dungeon: boxed text (David Hartlage, 2012-11-15)
claims.quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence

claims.claim: Gnome Stew (2008): in the 1980s reading boxed text aloud was 'considered a cardinal sin' among GMs, who were expected to paraphrase; the author later found reading helped immersion; commenters: 'Short box text is fine, long box text is a challenge.'
claims.source: Gnome Stew — Hot Button: Reading the Boxed Text (Walt Ciechanowski, 2008-12-18)
claims.quote: considered a cardinal sin

claims.claim: DM's Workshop: practice reading text aloud between sessions and match pacing to conversational speech; boxed text is a tool to adapt, not a script to recite.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)

claims.claim: Noonan's undercover Gen Con 2005 observation was that players attend to only the first two sentences of read-aloud boxed text before they start stacking dice or talking.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: If you're the DM, you get two sentences. Period.
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: Boxed text fails because it replaces the game's native conversational exchange (player asks, DM answers) with oration, which players are not used to listening to.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: Players repeatedly missed the concrete data embedded in boxed text (room dimensions, number of exits, number of monsters, who is a corpse), forcing DMs to repeat it mid-action.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: DMs read boxed text cold, from a script they have never spoken aloud, so even dynamic DMs deliver it flatly.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: Not a recipe for compelling delivery.
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: Noonan documents that WotC boxed text had already shortened by 2005, contrasting a three-sentence Sons of Gruumsh door entry with a paragraph-long 1999 Return to the Keep on the Borderlands cave entry.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: Noonan's advice to DMs is to ditch the boxed text and give the initial room description in their own words to keep the players in a conversation.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: ditch the boxed text and use your own words
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: In 2005 WotC R&D was actively testing alternatives to boxed text at the table, to appear in products if they played better.
claims.source: Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker & David Noonan, 2005-09-16)
claims.quote: We're goofing around with some alternatives right now.
claims.page: WotC designer column (read via Wayback text)

claims.claim: Noonan states an RPG book is first experienced by reading but lived by playing, so reading only yields an educated guess about quality.
claims.source: Design & Development: Reads Bad, Plays Good (David Noonan, 2006-06-16)
claims.quote: Reading a roleplaying book just lets you make an educated guess

claims.feature: metaplot prose reads well, plays badly
claims.claim: Mid-1990s campaign settings with intertwined factions and metaplots were great reads but hard to run because PCs became bit players.
claims.source: Design & Development: Reads Bad, Plays Good (David Noonan, 2006-06-16)
claims.quote: In short, they read good, played bad.

claims.claim: Pregenerated NPC stat blocks are no fun on a read-through but save the busy DM at the table, and WotC was working to make such material easier to find and use.
claims.source: Design & Development: Reads Bad, Plays Good (David Noonan, 2006-06-16)
claims.quote: They're no fun on a read-through.

claims.claim: RPGA/Living Greyhawk guidance forbids 'you', 'your' and 'you're' in read-aloud text because they seize control of the characters.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Dire Boxed Text (Craig Heir, RPGA/WotC, 2004-04-13)
claims.quote: Avoid the word "you" like the plague
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: Boxed text must not tell characters what they feel or do (crying babies bringing a tear to your eyes; grabbing your sword in fear); rewrite as a neutral scene the players react to.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Dire Boxed Text (Craig Heir, RPGA/WotC, 2004-04-13)
claims.quote: read aloud text does not run the character
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: Avoid long read-aloud passages in which NPCs carry on while the players sit idle; insert breaks for reactions.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Dire Boxed Text (Craig Heir, RPGA/WotC, 2004-04-13)
claims.quote: this is roleplaying not story time
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: Balance the amount of boxed text by running adventures to learn what is essential and cutting the rest; too much constrains the GM, too little strands them.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Dire Boxed Text (Craig Heir, RPGA/WotC, 2004-04-13)
claims.quote: Get a feel for what is bare-bones essential
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: A consistent style across RPGA adventures lets judges find information quickly; content and style rules live in the Living Greyhawk Writer's Guidelines.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Editor's Pen (Craig Heir, 2004-10-06)
claims.quote: allows judges to quickly find information they need
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: RPGA adventure content must stay PG-13 because children play the game.
claims.source: Living Greyhawk, Intro to Writing: Editor's Pen (Craig Heir, 2004-10-06)
claims.quote: keep your writing PG-13
claims.page: RPGA editor column on WotC site (read via Wayback)

claims.claim: Dungeon's read-aloud text gives a bare-bones description of the area and makes no reference to the viewer; 'you see' and 'as you enter the room' are banned.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: it does not make any reference to the viewer

claims.claim: Creatures are excluded from read-aloud text because their positions and activities depend on circumstances such as whether they heard the PCs.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: avoid including descriptions of any creatures in the room

claims.feature: few-sentence cap, handouts for the rest
claims.claim: Read-aloud text should only rarely exceed a few sentences; anything longer belongs in a player handout.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: should only rarely run more than a few sentences

claims.claim: Encounters are keyed with labeled sections in a fixed order (Read-aloud Text, General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Trap(s), Treasure, Development) and unneeded sections are omitted rather than filled.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: The editors greatly dislike printing the words "This room is empty"

claims.claim: The Adventure Background is capped at 5% of total length, with adventures running 5,000-15,000 words and about 10,000 preferred.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: no more than 5% of the total length

claims.claim: The mandatory synopsis must outline surprises and plot twists for the DM at the start rather than springing them during the adventure.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: Outline surprises and plot twists here

claims.claim: Sidebars are kept to a minimum and capped at 300 words because they take more page space than their word count suggests.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: no more than 300 words in length

claims.claim: Queries and adventures must condense backstory in favour of PC involvement; how the adventure plays decides acceptance.
claims.source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: an adventure is not a short story

claims.claim: Dragon refused articles written in the first person; 'I' and 'my' may appear only in a character's speech.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: we will not publish an article written in the first person

claims.claim: An opening narrative vignette or example dialogue may run no more than 200 words.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: no more than 200 words long

claims.claim: Writers are told to avoid passive writing and 'to be' verbs in particular.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: Especially avoid passive writing, particularly "to be" verbs

claims.claim: Magic item and spell names are italicized and feat names capitalized, following the current D&D product style.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: names of magic items and spells should be italicized

claims.claim: A Dragon page holds about 750 words and submissions should not exceed 5,000 words.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: A full page of text in DRAGON contains about 750 words

claims.claim: Failure to present information in D&D styles is listed alongside poor writing and imprecise mechanics as a standard rejection reason.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: failure to present information in D&D styles

claims.claim: Backgrounds and stories accompanying new rules must be interesting enough to stand alone without their rules element.
claims.source: Dragon Writers' Guidelines (Dragon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
claims.quote: interesting enough to stand alone without their rules element

claims.claim: Steve Winter applied newsroom training to TSR text: game language must be direct and clear, avoiding flowery phrases and clever wordplay.
claims.source: Grognardia: Interview: Steve Winter (2009-08-08)
claims.quote: the language needs to be direct and clear

claims.claim: A rulebook must decide up front whether it teaches newcomers or serves as a reference for people who know the fundamentals; it cannot do both.
claims.source: Grognardia: Interview: Steve Winter (2009-08-08)
claims.quote: I don't believe it can do both.

claims.claim: Mearls frames the game writer as a documentarian of an imaginary world who focuses on the props of a story: locations, characters, creatures, past events.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)
claims.quote: The writer as a documentarian of an imaginary world.

claims.claim: Game writing dwells on the kind of exposition that would bore a novel, little of which appears as-is in play.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)
claims.quote: the kind of exposition that can make a novel boring

claims.claim: Mechanics demand a lawyerly precision of language while setting text deliberately leaves gaps for the players' imagination.
claims.source: Mike Mearls of Dungeons & Dragons: Documenting Imaginary Worlds (SFWA, 2016-12-22)
claims.quote: a lawyerly approach to writing

claims.claim: Mearls' 2013 Legends & Lore column: rules terms exist to give abstract concepts a clear shared meaning, so '5th-level wizard' tells everyone what you can do.
claims.source: Legend & Lore says 'story not rules' (EN World thread quoting Mearls' 2013-03-04 column)
claims.quote: D&D is a shared language.

claims.claim: Mearls contrasts a self-explanatory descriptor like 'archer' with abstract feat names (Rapid Shot, Precise Shot) that can only be understood by already knowing them.
claims.source: Legend & Lore says 'story not rules' (EN World thread quoting Mearls' 2013-03-04 column)
claims.quote: They don't stand on their own in a meaningful way.

claims.claim: Perkins says he almost always overwrites; his first Dungeon adventure was cut from 28,000 to 16,000 words.
claims.source: An Interview with Chris Perkins, designer of Warriors of Heaven (Mimir.net, 1999)
claims.quote: I almost always overwrite

claims.claim: Perkins notes Planescape's slang was mostly absent from Warriors of Heaven and that he missed the pull-quotes that made those products fun to read.
claims.source: An Interview with Chris Perkins, designer of Warriors of Heaven (Mimir.net, 1999)
claims.quote: What I miss are the pull-quotes

claims.claim: Perkins recounts a 1992 Dungeon draft of 24,000 words cut to 15,000 as a cautionary tale about overwriting, and pitches Curse of Strahd's register as Gothic horror with a dash of dark fantasy.
claims.source: Curse of Strahd Interview with Chris Perkins (Fraternity of Shadows, Feb 2016)
claims.quote: a cautionary tale about overwriting

claims.claim: Perkins: adventures are meant to be read, so DM-facing text should be entertaining and bring a smile to the DM preparing.
claims.source: Chris Perkins on Writing your own Adventures (D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19, Todd Kenreck transcript)
claims.quote: make it entertaining

claims.claim: Perkins tells adventure writers to put puns, little laughs and Easter eggs in their text, embedded naturally rather than forced.
claims.source: Chris Perkins on Writing your own Adventures (D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19, Todd Kenreck transcript)
claims.quote: Put puns in your adventure.

claims.claim: Perkins warns against writing an adventure like a novel that dictates how each encounter must resolve; the text must survive unexpected choices and dice.
claims.source: Chris Perkins on Writing your own Adventures (D&D Beyond, 2018-04-19, Todd Kenreck transcript)

claims.claim: Perkins characterizes the original 1983 Ravenloft as economical in its writing yet rich in characterization, the model he expanded.
claims.source: Ex D&D boss Chris Perkins tells us why Strahd is the RPG's most successful villain (Wargamer, 2026-03-19)
claims.quote: economical

claims.claim: Wyatt set out to recapture the welcoming, teaching tone of the 4e DMG that the 2014 DMG lacked.
claims.source: D&D's James Wyatt & Chris Perkins Talk 2024 DM's Guide (CBR, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: the helpful tone to ease you in

claims.claim: Perkins found DMs did not know material existed in the 2014 DMG, so the 2024 text is organized to surface what is there.
claims.source: D&D's James Wyatt & Chris Perkins Talk 2024 DM's Guide (CBR, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: they didn't even know it was there

claims.claim: Wyatt wrote the 2024 DMG's examples of play as scripts of the game unfolding to show how it functions.
claims.source: D&D's James Wyatt & Chris Perkins Talk 2024 DM's Guide (CBR, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: presenting the scripts of that unfolding in play

claims.claim: The 2024 DMG front-loads basic information about DMing and moves world creation to the middle, mirroring the PHB's structure.
claims.source: Chris Perkins and James Wyatt Answer Burning Questions About the 2024 DMG, page 2 (EN World, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: front-loading all of the basic information

claims.claim: Wyatt names the 2014 DMG's organization as its biggest drawback and says a DMG should guide you on how to be a DM.
claims.source: Chris Perkins and James Wyatt Answer Burning Questions About the 2024 DMG, page 2 (EN World, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: the organization of the 2014 DMG was its biggest drawback

claims.claim: Every published WotC adventure opens by explaining what boxed text is; with the 2024 DMG defining it on p. 9, Wyatt wants to drop that boilerplate.
claims.source: After DM's Guide Preview, Future D&D Adventures Will Drop These Two Repetitive Features (Screen Rant, 2024-10-29)
claims.quote: tells you what boxed text is

claims.claim: Perkins says re-explaining doors in every adventure bothered him for a decade; the 2024 DMG's doors page lets adventures stop repeating it.
claims.source: After DM's Guide Preview, Future D&D Adventures Will Drop These Two Repetitive Features (Screen Rant, 2024-10-29)
claims.quote: super, super important

claims.claim: Abadia (AL admin): dropping boxed text does not remove the need to tell the DM what to convey; the test is whether information reaches the DM.
claims.source: The Best and Worst of Adventure Formats at Winter Fantasy 2020 (Teos Abadia, Alphastream, 2020-02-20)
claims.quote: the DM still needs some way to understand what to convey

claims.claim: AL Season 8's rigid template scattered one animated door's description across Dimensions & Terrain, Door and Creatures/NPCs sections, obscuring intent.
claims.source: The Best and Worst of Adventure Formats at Winter Fantasy 2020 (Teos Abadia, Alphastream, 2020-02-20)
claims.quote: You must read both places

claims.claim: The AL 'Playing the Pillars' sidebars existed to exist and added little value.
claims.source: The Best and Worst of Adventure Formats at Winter Fantasy 2020 (Teos Abadia, Alphastream, 2020-02-20)
claims.quote: It exists sort of just to exist

claims.claim: Abadia finds the 2025 Monster Manual devotes far fewer words to describing monsters and less actionable encounter information than 2014's inspiring lore.
claims.source: Best and Worst of the Revised Monster Manual (Teos Abadia, Alphastream, 2025-03-13)
claims.quote: far fewer words devoted to describing the monster

claims.claim: 2025 Multiattack lines inconsistently include 'in any combination', and the gelatinous cube's codified wording is harder to understand than before.
claims.source: Best and Worst of the Revised Monster Manual (Teos Abadia, Alphastream, 2025-03-13)
claims.quote: a fair lack of clarity in monster stat blocks

claims.claim: Baur: beginners want full support (all stats, contingencies, corner cases) while veterans want bullet lists and bare-bones text with wiggle room.
claims.source: Compiling Wolfgang Baur's AMA (EN World, 2015-06-03)
claims.quote: bullet lists, bare bones text that allows them to improvise

claims.claim: Baur's writing advice to designers is to turn out a lot of prose.
claims.source: Compiling Wolfgang Baur's AMA (EN World, 2015-06-03)
claims.quote: Speed keeps you fed; quality keeps you respected.

claims.claim: Baur (ex-Dungeon editor) says most history is wasted energy; keep backstory recent and relevant and avoid openings of 'Thousands of years ago'.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)
claims.quote: avoid anything that starts "Thousands of years ago..."

claims.claim: The four errors Baur saw constantly at Dungeon: too much useless backstory, slow starts, random encounters, too many encounters.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)
claims.quote: too much useless backstory

claims.claim: Involved history that the PCs cannot learn belongs in sourcebooks, not adventures.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)
claims.quote: Save that for sourcebooks.

claims.claim: Hooks must be specific and hard to refuse; vague or cliched openings (stranger in a tavern, request from the mayor) fail.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Setting the Hook, Part 2 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-08-11)
claims.quote: Vague, overused, or clichéd hooks don't interest players

claims.claim: Baur borrows fiction's inciting incident: an arrow with an Elvish note shot into camp beats a guy in a bar.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Setting the Hook, Part 2 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-08-11)
claims.quote: In fiction, it would be called the "inciting incident."

claims.feature: design labels kept out of game text
claims.claim: Noonan deliberately used modern-sounding monster role labels (mook, artillery, decathlete) so they would not creep into published game text.
claims.source: Design & Development: How to Make a Monster Manual, Part 1 (David Noonan, 2007-07-27)
claims.quote: I didn't want the roles to creep into game text

claims.claim: Monster entries are not allowed to break across page spreads, which limits text length and illustration size.
claims.source: Design & Development: How to Make a Monster Manual, Part 1 (David Noonan, 2007-07-27)
claims.quote: monsters don't break out of page spreads

claims.claim: Rich Baker, reviewing his own TSR adventures, calls his heavy use of boxed text a 2e-era style thing.
claims.source: Baker's Field: Twenty-Eight Adventures (Part 1) (Richard Baker, 2015-03-09)
claims.quote: kind of a 2e style thing

claims.claim: WotC scheduled adventure writing in 'MU' units of 32 pages or 20,000-22,000 words, about one designer-month each.
claims.source: Baker's Field: Twenty-Eight Adventures (Part 1) (Richard Baker, 2015-03-09)

claims.claim: WotC freelancers in 2012 were held to the Chicago Manual of Style and required to deliver manuscripts in WotC's Word templates needing minimal grammar or syntax editing.
claims.source: Freelancer Chronicles: The Coast Wizards and I, Some Lessons (Critical Hits, 2012-12-19)
claims.quote: that's going to be your main bible

claims.claim: The WotC Adventure Guide, as quoted by Shea, instructs writers to focus on the here and now and omit verbose backstories.
claims.source: On Writing Adventures (Mike Shea, Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17)
claims.quote: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories
claims.page: compilation of designer advice incl. WotC Adventure Guide

claims.claim: Kobold Guide precepts quoted by Shea: small beats large, be specific, read your work aloud.
claims.source: On Writing Adventures (Mike Shea, Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17)
claims.quote: Small beats large. Keep it brief
claims.page: compilation of designer advice incl. WotC Adventure Guide

claims.claim: Greenwood says shared-world writers must fit in, perhaps even to a particular prose style, without contradicting existing lore.
claims.source: Making the Realms Shine: A Conversation with Ed Greenwood, Part I (Kobold Press, 2009)
claims.quote: perhaps even to a particular prose style

claims.claim: Greenwood writes by imagining he is present, smelling and tasting what characters do, then writing down enough for the reader to see the crypt or court.
claims.source: Making the Realms Shine: A Conversation with Ed Greenwood, Part I (Kobold Press, 2009)
claims.quote: I'm smelling what the characters are smelling

claims.claim: Greenwood writes what publishers ask for, in the way they want it, and still entertainingly.
claims.source: Making the Realms Shine: A Conversation with Ed Greenwood, Part I (Kobold Press, 2009)
claims.quote: I write about what publishers ask me to

claims.claim: Greenwood's advice: never think your words are perfect; rewrite anything weak or awkward.
claims.source: Author Interview: Ed Greenwood (Paizo Blog, 2013-06-20)
claims.quote: Never think your words are perfect

claims.claim: Crawford reads a rule first as written, in context and without regard to intent, because the published text must stand on its own.
claims.source: Sage Advice Compendium (Jeremy Crawford, Wizards of the Coast, v2.7 2021)
