CAVEAT: the guide permits any terminal punctuation - 'Use a period, an exclamation point, or a question mark' - so 'end in a period' is narrower than the rule.

4.trueWording: Numerals in Rules. In rules writing, we use numerals more often.
4.note: Every example in the claim is verbatim in the source: 'Anyone who touches the orb regains 3 hit points'; 'The spell lasts for 1 round'; 'The attack has a range of 30 feet'; and under 'But:' - 'The two cities are fifty miles apart' and 'After winning the fight, the characters slept for six hours.' The general rule cited is Chicago 9.2 (spell out zero to one hundred). 'always' is a shade stronger than the guide's framing but the substance holds.

5.trueWording: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails.
5.note: Page 6 'Verb Usage' list carries all of it verbatim: 'You deal damage.' / 'You take damage.' / 'You regain hit points.' / 'You make an attack (or you attack), and your attack hits or misses (it doesn't succeed or fail).' CAVEAT on 'must succeed on (not must make)': the ban is conditional - 'Don't write, "You must make a DC 15 Strength check..." unless that sentence is immediately followed by a description of what happens on a success or failure.' Separately, for effects imposing a save the guide actually PREFERS 'the target must make a saving throw'.

6.note: The sentence appears twice, verbatim, once for each abandonment: under 'Saving Throws' ('In 4E, we used "save" as a synonym for "successful saving throw." We have abandoned that practice.') and under '"Result" and Die Rolls' ('In 3E and 4E, the word "result" was sometimes used as a synonym for "the number rolled on a die." We have abandoned that practice.'). Also confirmed: '"magic item" and its variants should never be "magical item"'; 'write, "The spell deals 10 fire damage," not "The spell deals 10 points of fire damage"'; 'When you write about a creature's hit point maximum, avoid "maximum hit points."'

7.trueWording: The italicized terms are treated as titles, even when they don't use title capitalization.
7.note: 'Terms to Capitalize' lists Ability scores, Armor Class, Artifacts, Class features, Difficulty Class, Dungeon Master, Feats, Languages, Planes of existence, Skills, Traits. 'Terms to Italicize' lists Artifacts, Magic items, Spells. The distinctness point is verbatim: 'Don't confuse one of these titles with an effect it creates... the wall of fire spell produces a wall of fire, not a wall of fire.' Note artifacts are BOTH capitalized and italicized.

8.trueWording: there are moments of humor with the hobbits, but ring wraiths aren't used for gags
8.note: Quote is verbatim apart from the source's curly apostrophe in 'aren't'. The 'High Fantasy' section confirms epic scope ('the epic scope characteristic of that subgenre') and teamwork ('The lone knight fighting a dragon is less characteristic of D&D than an adventuring team fighting a dragon'). CAVEAT: the LotR/Game of Thrones test is framed as a 'When in doubt' heuristic, not the permission condition - the stated condition is that humor/tragedy be 'true to the facts of the brand and don't overtake the general tone'. 'The only prose-tone guidance' is the reviewer's inference, but it survives a read of all 9 pages: no other voice or register section exists.

9.note: All six sub-claims confirmed verbatim: 'We use American style for spelling and punctuation'; the serial-comma sentence; 'We write "Asmodeus's lair," not "Asmodeus' lair"'; 'non-elf, non-dwarf, non-orc, non-drow (but nonhuman, as in Webster's)'; 'We encourage the use of contractions formed with "not"'; 'introduce it with a complete sentence ended by a colon' for vertical lists.

10.trueWording: We avoid page references as much as possible.
10.note: Continues 'They are labor-intensive (they must be added by hand during galley review), and they invite error.' Cross-reference style confirmed: 'When you refer to a chapter, use its number' and 'When you refer to a subsection, including a sidebar, use its title in quotes.' One refinement: a table title is explicitly NOT enclosed in quotes.

11.trueWording: Read-aloud text provides a bare-bones description of the encounter area; it does not make any reference to the viewer.
11.note: Verbatim on the page (page 12-13 boundary); my PDF text extractor merely dropped the space at the 'it / does' line break. Next sentence is verbatim too: 'Avoid phrases such as "you see," "as you enter the room," or other phrases that assume any action whatsoever on behalf of the players.' Paizo attribution confirmed by the document itself: byline 'By the DUNGEON Staff', address 'DUNGEON Magazine, Paizo Publishing, 2700 Richards Road, Suite 201, Bellevue, WA'. Era is 3.5e (cites Monster Manual II, Fiend Folio, Draconomicon, DUNGEON #114).

12.trueWording: Read-aloud text for an encounter should only rarely run more than a few sentences.
12.note: Both halves verbatim and adjacent: 'You should also avoid including descriptions of any creatures in the room, since their activities and positions in the room often depend on multiple factors (such as if they hear the PCs coming, if it's night or day, and so on).' and 'Long sections of read-aloud text are better served as player handouts.'

13.trueWording: Read-aloud Text, General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Trap(s), Treasure, Development, and Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment
13.note: Quote IS verbatim ('This section generally precedes the other entries of an encounter, although part of the general description might precede it if important to the encounter.'), and the header/EL and word-count halves are confirmed verbatim: 'Each encounter should be rated with an Encounter Level (EL #) in the main encounter header'; sample header '23. Vampire's Den (EL 13)'; 'Our adventures typically range from 5,000 to 15,000 words in length'; 'we automatically reject any adventure manuscript that contains fewer than 5,000 or more than 15,000 words. The ideal manuscript size is 10,000 words.' DOWNGRADED because the claim's section order is wrong: the source order is Treasure BEFORE Development, and the claim omits Trap(s) and Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment from a list it presents as the template. Also 'mandatory Read-Aloud Text' needs care - the heading is labelled (Mandatory) in the template, but the encounters paragraph says 'Each encounter can include any or all of the following sections... Do not include sections that are unnecessary for a given encounter.'

14.trueWording: Regardless of how cool your backstory is, an adventure is not a short story.
14.note: Quote verbatim in the query-writing tips. Continues: 'You need to condense or sacrifice background description in favor of telling us about PC involvement. It's how the adventure PLAYS that determines whether or not a proposal is something we want to pick up.' The anti-railroad half is verbatim elsewhere: 'Avoid excessively linear plots that force the story toward an inevitable conclusion or "railroad" the actions of the PCs. The adventure should be flexible enough for PCs to make choices and decisions that could affect the outcome of the story. Avoid rigid timelines.' The design guide adds 'The Adventure Background section should be no more than 5% of the total length of the adventure.'

15.trueWording: Tip 5. Read your boxed text aloud to check readability
15.note: Quote verbatim (Tip 5 heading). Every element confirmed on the page: 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words.'; third-person example replacing 'As you enter the clearing, you notice the bloated corpse of a headless dragon'; Tip 3 'Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they can't'; boxed text criticised when it 'assumes a character's feelings, movements, actions, or reactions'; the four-paragraph villain 'boxed-text monologue' criticised; Tip 6 'Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way'. Byline 'by Shawn Merwin / Nov 6, 2019' matches. Fetched by WebFetch and re-fetched raw by curl (HTTP 200).

16.trueWording: Everything they sense “appears to be” what it is.
16.note: Word-for-word match; only the inner quotation marks differ (page uses curly double quotes, the claim renders them single). Full context: 'Tip 4. Avoid “seems to be” or “appears to be.” For the characters, perception is reality.' Supports the claim that boxed text should describe only what characters perceive without hedging.

17.trueWording: if they come away from reading that adventure, having had a few good laughs, they're much more inclined to run it
17.note: Quote verbatim, spoken by Chris Perkins. Also verbatim on the page: 'if you are going to make somebody read something for **** sakes', make it entertaining'; 'Put puns in your adventure. Put little laughs. Put little Easter eggs in your adventure.'; and 'the bait has to be something that is generally applicable ... maybe 80 or 90% of players are going to latch onto'. Byline 'by Todd Kenreck / Apr 19, 2018' matches. Note: the 80-90% line is about the adventure hook/bait, exactly as claimed.

18.trueWording: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories.
18.note: Quote verbatim as one bullet in the article's 'D&D House Style Guide' list. Companion bullets read 'Focus on the importance of the characters.' and 'Include a solid credible threat.' — the claim's shortened wording is a fair summary, not the page's exact words. Framing confirmed: 'This free set of documents from Wizards of the Coast includes the house styles the D&D team gives to freelancers.' Byline 'by Mike on 17 June 2019' matches.

19.trueWording: Read the boxed text when you’re ready to start.
19.note: Quote verbatim (curly apostrophe) inside Appendix B, 'B Lost Mine of Phadelver Adventure', of the EMNLP 2022 paper (Callison-Burch, Tomar, Martin, Ippolito et al.). The definition is also verbatim: 'The adventure book provides boxed text, which is descriptive text to be read aloud verbatim or to paraphrase. It also gives details about the combat ... and links to relevant [rules]'; and the skip instruction follows: 'If you create a different adventure hook, skip to the second paragraph'. Paper title is 'Dialog Challenge', not 'Dialogue Challenge' — trivial. Verified by extracting the PDF text locally (15 pages).

20.trueWording: Hints of what may be done are given in this text and the DM should only provide vague information if questioned.
20.note: Quote verbatim (the article quoting The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan). Confirmed: 'Read-aloud text is analogous to “at rise” descriptions.' and 'D&D adventure writers employ descriptive text in the same way as playwrights use “at rise” descriptions'; 'because it is typically set outside from the other text in a box'; 'the 1980 adventure module The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan marks its first appearance.' One gloss unsupported: the word 'verbatim' never appears in the article — it says the DM 'is instructed to read' the boxed text to players. Byline 'December 18, 2023 Brian McKenzie' matches.

21.trueWording: The results were 59.5% desired “occasional boxed text,” 34.4% “lots of boxed text,” and only 6% of respondents did not want any boxed text.
21.note: All three figures and the phrase 'occasional boxed text' verbatim. Attribution confirmed: 'A Twitter poll by D&D's current lead rules designer Jeremy Crawford saw 2,248 replies to the question “How much boxed text (aka read-aloud text) do you like in an adventure you run?”' (endnote 38 cites @JeremyECrawford, 17 Nov 2016). The claim's 'about 6%' matches 'only 6%'.

22.trueWording: read aloud text that the DM is instructed to read to the players. Often these passages describe the location, but sometimes they are also used to describe the action of NPCs
22.note: Google Books snippet for p.64 of Cover's book carries the quoted fragment word for word plus the location/NPC-action distinction. The cut-scene comparison is on the adjacent snippets: p.65 '... read aloud in the TRPG, but add more visual interest. Cut-scenes are moments in a videogames where the gameplay is interrupted by a visual scene' and p.66 '... read aloud text in the module. The opening of the computer game is a fairly elaborate cut-scene'. Cited pages 64-66 and 80 all return snippets. Route note: WebFetch of the URL returned metadata only; the snippets came from the same URL fetched raw with curl (HTTP 200), whose embedded JSON holds four search_results.

23.trueWording: second-person, pulling them directly into the storyworld, situating them in a place, and immersing them.
23.note: Quote verbatim in the Google Books snippet, together with 'situating' and 'immersing'. Fludernik is confirmed at p.85: 'Monik Fludernik (1994) explains that “second person texts frequently undermine this story-discourse dichotomy by the very nonnaturalness of their design...”'. Caveat: the immersion sentence sits on p.107, not on pp.21/85 as the source field cites; p.21 discusses second person and audience address, p.85 the Fludernik narratology. Same curl route as index 22.

24.trueWording: the frequency that words like “tribal,” “exotic,” and “savage” crop up throughout the module
24.note: Both halves confirmed. Loaded adjectives verbatim as quoted. Port Nyanzaru: 'the first instance of “flavor text”, or text that the Dungeon Master is explicitly meant to read aloud to the players, highlights dinosaurs, “Minstrels in bright clothing,” and voices speaking “in an unfamiliar language filled with clicks.” Here, we begin to see how the module gestures towards vague stereotypes of the African diaspora'. The claim's quote field ('heavy, characteristic accent') is also verbatim on the page, though it belongs to the DM-guidance sentence (index 25) rather than the Port Nyanzaru passage. Byline 'March 19, 2023 Mark Hines' matches.

25.trueWording: encouraging players to adopt a certain mentality or approach
25.note: First half verified verbatim: 'the game's only guidance in portraying Chultans is to emphasize “tongue clicks” and their “heavy, characteristic accent.”' The quoted fragment 'correctly ascertain its original purpose' is also verbatim. But the claim's characterisation is the claimant's gloss, not Hines's: he presents it as the Archaeologist *background's mechanical feature* (an identity mechanic), arguing it caters to 'dungeons that combine race and place' and is 'meant to evoke images and stereotype in the minds of players' — he never calls it prose and never says ruins need outsider validation. Downgraded for that gap only.

26.trueWording: gothic atmosphere clearly set through the statue and skeletal remains
26.note: The Death House passage is quoted verbatim on the page — 'This room is festooned with moldy skeletons that hang from rusty shackles against the walls... a gaunt, pale-faced man wearing a voluminous black cloak' — so all five adjectives are present, and Hewitt does say 'The gothic atmosphere is clearly set through the daunting presence of the statue, as well as the skeletal remains lurking in the corners of the room.' What the article does NOT do is what the claim credits it with: it introduces the passage as 'The suggested description', never uses the terms 'read-aloud' or 'boxed text' (zero occurrences), and makes no argument about decay adjectives, present tense, or third person. The adjective/tense/person analysis is the claimant's, not Hewitt's. Byline 'December 15, 2024 Meghan Hewitt' matches.

27.trueWording: “double use” of framing devices was notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs
27.note: Quote verbatim in the full-text PDF (journals.uu.se/IJRP/article/download/228/252/576), in the passage 'by observing the simplicity of the original cover of the D&D game from 1974 (See fig. 3), it becomes evident that the aforementioned “double use” of framing devices was notoriously less prominent in early TRPGs'. The storytelling-game prologue point is also explicit: 'practically all of them begin with a prologue consisting of a short narrative text that provides an atmospheric introduction into the fictional setting'. The abstract names 'cover illustrations, prologues and epilogues' as the paratexts studied; section 3.3.2 covers 'Prologues, Epilogues and Framing/Embedded Narratives'. Note: the source's comparison is specifically the covers' double (typographic + pictorial) framing, not framing in general.

28.trueWording: the use of framings in TRPGs to incite the production (and not only the reception) of text is what I have called genesic framing
28.note: Quote verbatim, in the conclusion and repeated as a pull-quote. Self-disclosure element confirmed ('of self-disclosure, as well as the use of framings...'), as is the persistence element: 'it is this feature that is likely to account for much of the complexity of the TRPG medium as well as for its persistence in time.' The source hedges with 'likely to account for much of', where the claim says flatly 'accounts for'.

29.trueWording: the first edition’s visual–textual dissonance produces interpretive ambiguity that might enhance embodied player engagement
29.note: ROUTE: journals.sagepub.com returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and a browser-UA curl, and the Wayback availability API reports no snapshot for this DOI, so the Sage page itself is unreachable. Verified instead against the publisher-deposited abstract for the same DOI via the Crossref API (HTTP 200): title 'Tomes and Tombs: Toward a Phenomenology of Interiors in Dungeons & Dragons', author Cameron Macdonell, published online 2025-09-03. That abstract carries the claim's quote word for word, and also 'Later editions increasingly removed visual assets'. Unconfirmed at abstract level (full text paywalled, as the claim itself concedes): the year 1978 and the specific 'illustration booklet'; the abstract says 'the first edition' and 'visual assets', and hedges with 'might enhance'.

30.trueWording: using the passive voice a lot, the occasional stream-of-consciousness digressions
30.note: Live fetch 200. Quote is word for word in Cook's own sentence, which continues 'an advanced vocabulary (I was a 14-year-old who used terms like "weal or woe" because of Gary), and a very authoritative tone.' The treatise/legitimacy element is also explicit: 'Reading Gary's AD&D Dungeon Master's Guide was like reading a treatise on some vital topic of complexity and depth' and 'it was meaningful to read someone treating the activity we loved as seriously as a scholar would' / 'We felt that it was both validating and compelling.' Claim fully supported.

31.trueWording: use a platinum word when one worth a copper would do
31.note: Live fetch 200. Quote appears word for word BUT in the comment thread, not the post body - it is a reader's line, which Maliszewski then quotes back approvingly ('That's very well put!', Feb 20 2009 8:31 AM). Post body does support: 'the baroque splendor of High Gygaxian speech', 'Gygax at his florid best', the assassin-alignment example with 'perforce' and 'antithesis of weal', 'his lifelong love of dictionaries and thesauruses', and the Vault of the Drow passage as the fullest form ('not until later that it reaches its fullest flower'). THREE sub-claims NOT supported by this page: (a) that Maliszewski COINED 'High Gygaxian' - the post uses the term as already current and makes no coinage claim; (b) 'fullest in the 1979 DMG' - the DMG appears only in a reader comment, never in the post body; (c) 'long multi-clause sentences' - the post never characterises sentence length.

32.trueWording: you had to be smarter than average to understand it
32.note: Live fetch 200. Quote is word for word on the page, but MISATTRIBUTED: it is inside a block quote Akrasia reproduces from 'this post by Trent Foster from 2009', introduced as making 'essentially this point (though far better than I could)'. The Latinate-difficulty examples in that block are Foster's ('milieu' and 'antithesis of weal'); the words 'dweomer', 'phantasm', 'eldritch', 'milieux', 'melee' appear only in Akrasia's own COMMENT reply (20 March 2013), not the post body. The TSR-simplification element is likewise Foster's: 'When TSR started changing the game around -- making it more kid-friendly by simplifying the language and sanitizing the content ... the appeal was lost'. Akrasia's own voice does endorse the thesis: 'Gygax's idiosyncratic writing style actually was part of AD&D's appeal 30+ years ago, not a barrier to it.'

33.trueWording: Gygax was good at short punchy bits of detail
33.note: Live fetch 200. Quote word for word. 'precipitated' element verbatim: 'Characters aren't dropped or deposited on floors by trapdoors, they are \'precipitated\' for example', in 'that thesaurus lover with a somewhat lacking education style'. Re-reading element supported: 'This writing style is also confusing, with information design that requires multiple re-reads to grasp.' ONE sub-claim NOT supported: 'room text that mixes mechanics with narrative' is nowhere on the page - the review names confusing information design, never a mechanics/narrative blend, and never discusses room or read-aloud text structure.

34.trueWording: The Dungeon Master's Guide is strange and deeply idiosyncratic
34.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word inside the Horvath quotation, cited to Monsters, Aliens, and Holes in the Ground (MIT Press, 2023, p. 58); continues 'Gygax expresses in it a singular vision that feels true'. Wieck element verbatim: 'it has become as much a guide of advice for Dungeon Masters as a manual of specific information' (White Wolf #17, 1989). Taylor element verbatim: 'The 5E DMG devotes the first 127 pages to teaching a novice player how to [be] a Dungeon Master in this system' (Black Gate). All three sub-claims supported.

35.trueWording: the spell section was an unrelenting wall of text
35.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word (Benjamin Abbott, GamesRadar+, August 20 2024, about the 2014 edition). Turnbull element verbatim: 'whereas the original rules are ambiguous and muddled, the Handbook is a detailed and coherent game-system, and very sophisticated' - but the ref dates that review White Dwarf #10, December 1978 - January 1979, so '(1978)' is only approximately right. Schick element verbatim: spell descriptions 'have positively bloated to over 100 pages' (Heroic Worlds, 1991). Kelly element verbatim: 'the writing is much more polished' (GeekDad, August 18 2014). All four sub-claims supported.

36.trueWording: modeled after medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures
36.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word: 'Games scholar Jaroslav Svelch saw the Monster Manual modeled after "medieval bestiaries, only with more precise figures"' (Monster Culture in the 21st Century, Bloomsbury, 2013, p. 197). Turnbull element verbatim: he 'praised the explanatory text, stating that it "amplifies, where necessary, [the game statistics] and the result is the most comprehensive listing of D&D monsters you will find"' (White Dwarf #8, Aug-Sep 1978). Both sub-claims supported.

37.trueWording: there is no depth to their listings
37.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word. Structure element verbatim: the 1977 book 'expanded on the original monster format by including the stat lines on the same page as the monsters' descriptions'. Greenwood element present but NARROWER than the claim: the article has him considering 'the hook horror as one of the creatures with "strange appearances and little else; there is no depth to their listings"' in his Fiend Folio review (Dragon #55, November 1981) - a remark about a subset of creatures, which the claim generalises to 'Fiend Folio entries'.

38.trueWording: It is the first D&D adventure to use boxed, read aloud text
38.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word. Sourcing element confirmed: the sentence's only citation is {{Cite web |last=B |first=Merric |date=4 May 2017 |title=AD&D Adventure Review: The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan |website=Merric's Musings}} - a single 2017 blog post, not a scholarly source, exactly as the claim says. The ref gives the author as 'Merric B', not 'Merric Blackman', so the surname in the claim comes from outside this page.

39.trueWording: sounds more like a cranky Redditor than a fantastical crime boss
39.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word: 'Xanathar's voice, as applied in this book, feels a bit too modern. He sounds more like a cranky Redditor than a fantastical crime boss' (Charlie Hall, Polygon, 2017-11-13). Two wording drifts in the claim: it says 'Reviewers' plural when the article cites only Hall for this point, and renders 'fantastical crime boss' as 'fantasy crime lord' (the article does separately call Xanathar 'a powerful crime lord in the city of Waterdeep').

40.trueWording: having Volo write the guide means that he can be wrong
40.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word (the source has wiki italic markup around 'wrong', which renders identically). Kunzelman/Paste element supported: 'Volo is a device through which the designers of the Forgotten Realms can give Dungeon Masters a set of bounds ... Whatever Volo thinks or writes can be slightly off the mark'; the 'rumor and error' framing is explicit in his later review, which faults the book because it 'mostly tells the DM facts about a world, rather than opinions, rumors and suspicions that might be completely unfounded'. Furniss element verbatim: 'I love the marriage of narrative and mechanical information' (Destructoid, 16 November 2016).

41.trueWording: like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book from front to back
41.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. NOT verbatim: the claim's quote drops 'from'. The page reads 'it was a bit like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book from front to back, rather than following the breadcrumbs' (Rory Bristol, GeekDad, 2016-03-15). Substance otherwise supported, including the second element verbatim: Andrew Zimmerman Jones in Black Gate said Curse of Strahd 'is really a mix of setting manual and adventure module in one'.

42.trueWording: terminology and choices should be immediately intelligible to all
42.note: Wikipedia wikitext via Special:Export. Quote word for word inside Torner's sentence: 'D&D 3e and 3.5e bear the influence of Eurogame-style elegant design: that the terminology and choices in the game should be immediately intelligible to all who might play it', with the designers' aim given as to 'simplify and declutter the whole system'. Cited to Evan Torner, 'Combat In Dungeons & Dragons', Fifty Years of Dungeons & Dragons (MIT Press, 2024). Claim fully supported.

43.trueWording: just being used in their normal sense
43.note: Live site refused with HTTP 403; verified through the Wayback Machine snapshot 20251219191134 of the same URL. Quote word for word under heading '8. Capitalising Game Mechanics In The Text': 'It really is a crime that the 2014 Player's Handbook left DMs to work out if certain words were just being used in their normal sense or if they referred to some mechanic in the game. Thankfully that mistake wasn't repeated in 2024.' Glossary element supported under '2. Handy Rules Glossary': 'a dedicated rules glossary covering basically everything you need in an a-z of mechanics at the back of the book'. All three sub-claims supported.

44.trueWording: Cast a Spell action -> Magic action
44.note: Live fetch 200. 'Magic action' word for word in the Updated Terminology table, which also carries every other rename in the claim: Race -> Species, Cast a Spell action -> Magic action, Inspiration -> Heroic Inspiration, Use an Object action -> Utilize action, and Shoving -> Unarmed Strike. The 'New Rules' list of the 2024 Rules Glossary includes Ally, Bloodied, Enemy and Passive Perception (the glossary spells the action entry 'Magic (action)'). All sub-claims supported.

45.trueWording: the lack of a dedicated section for Conditions
45.note: Quote appears word for word: 'Tossing so much into one glossary does come with certain drawbacks, like the need to reference the back of the book more frequently while learning the basic rules and the lack of a dedicated section for Conditions.' The art clause is also verbatim on the page: 'the Rules Glossary is also the one part of DnD's 2024 Player's Handbook that largely de-emphasizes artwork, squeezing monochrome scenes into banners at the top of some pages but devoting most of the real estate to the text.' Both halves of the claim confirmed. Fetched via WebFetch, HTTP 200.

46.trueWording: three paragraphs and a table to roll on
46.note: Quote verbatim: 'Creatures like Aboleths, Beholders, and Mind Flayers from multi-page descriptions that show you their backstory and place in the world to, at best, three paragraphs and a table to roll on.' All three remaining sub-assertions confirmed on the page: subtitles — 'they also all now have Dark Souls boss subtitles' (article's word is 'subtitles', not 'epithet'); phylactery — 'Instead of the Greek word Phylactery ... the Monster Manual now uses "spirit jar."'; utilitarian encyclopedia — 'It goes from an in-universe collection of monster lore to a glorified encyclopedia. It's stripped down to something purely utilitarian.' Byline and date in page JSON-LD match the citation exactly: author 'Dan Arndt', datePublished 2025-01-28. WebFetch returned HTTP 403; retrieved via curl with a browser user agent, HTTP 200, 289,672 bytes.

47.note: The cited academia.edu page does not contain the quoted phrase or any supporting text. Direct fetch 403s (WebFetch and curl); the Wayback snapshot 20250914225534 fetched successfully (HTTP 200, 196,401 bytes) and is a login-walled listing page whose only body text is metadata ('Master's Thesis: The Narrative Structures of Dungeons and Dragons', '2011', 'Nathan Shank'), download prompts, related-paper links, and 'Sorry, preview is currently unavailable. You can download the paper by clicking the button above.' Zero occurrences of 'encyclopedic', 'geography', 'ancillary' or 'campaign setting' in the retrieved text. Not BLOCKED — the page was retrieved; it simply carries no abstract. An exact-phrase web search for the quotation surfaced no verbatim match anywhere. The thesis may well say this in its PDF body, but nothing at the cited URL supports it, so the citation as written is unverifiable and needs the PDF itself.

48.note: The claim is a self-declared negative result; its 'source' field names the sweep's own searches, not the URL. The cited arXiv page (2210.07109, 'Dungeons and Dragons as a Dialog Challenge for Artificial Intelligence') was fetched successfully and does confirm the one clause that touches it — it is an actual-play dialogue NLP dataset ('a gameplay dataset consisting of nearly 900 games ... 800,000 dialogue turns ... 58 million words'), not stylometry or authorship attribution, so the citation is correctly characterised. But no single page can establish the load-bearing existential negative (that no stylometric/corpus study of official D&D prose exists, and that 'Gygaxian' is absent from three journal indexes), and the arXiv page asserts nothing about it. Two adversarial counter-searches (stylometry/corpus/authorship-attribution of D&D rulebook prose; 'Gygaxian' across AGS, Games and Culture, IJRP) surfaced no refuting study, so the negative is not contradicted — it is merely unestablished by the cited source. Verify this row by index searches, not by source fetch.
